TEACHER RESEARCH NOTES · 27 OCTOBER 2026

What the Grade 7 sample questions actually ask learners to do

This report reviews the 11 supplied photographs and an accessible Chinese sample-paper preview. The photographs show more than one paper, photographed at different angles; some material is cropped. This is an instructional analysis, not a formal diagnosis, complete transcription or verified rescore. Handwritten names, contact details, school identifiers and the original photographs are excluded from this public report.

1. The papers test several different skills

Visible question typeWhat it demandsTeaching response
Pronunciation, word stress and sentence stressSound–spelling links, syllable emphasis and emphasis that answers a question.Hear and distinguish sounds, then read phrases aloud. Printed phonetic symbols alone are insufficient.
Everyday dialogue and single-choice language useChoose an appropriate greeting, a word that fits the situation, or a conventional expression.Practise response pairs, collocations and context; explain why distractors do not fit.
Word bank with form changes; mixed grammatical gapsIdentify the part of speech and role required, then supply the right pronoun, verb ending, adjective or adverb.Separate meaning recognition from form selection and typed recall.
Passage cloze and sentence insertionCoordinate grammar, reference, vocabulary, contrast/cause and whole-text coherence.Move from one clue to two linked sentences, then a short paragraph with several gaps.
Reading details, inference, context meaning and structureLocate evidence, infer cautiously, identify paragraph functions and distinguish a main purpose from one detail.Ask learners to point to evidence and explain the connection, not only choose a letter.
Task-based reading and restricted-length answersTransform information: calculate a total or duration, identify a category, and meet a word limit.Teach question words, answer units and final checking explicitly.
Short writing from a mind map or email promptCover the requested content, maintain pronoun/verb accuracy, connect sentences and check spelling.Plan with a map, build accurate sentence frames, then produce and revise a short message.

2. Patterns worth teaching from the marked work

The word-bank exercise about a friend and family contains several appropriately formed responses. Other marked gaps and the short message show errors with grammatical function and spelling. These observations justify targeted practice; they do not establish that the learner has mastered or failed an entire language area.

  • Subject versus possession: compare “She is friendly” with “Her name is…”. A possessive form cannot replace a subject merely because both refer to the same person.
  • Word class: a person can be “friendly”; an action can be done “happily”. Teach the role a word fills in the sentence before changing its ending.
  • Verb patterns: compare want to do, spend time doing and make someone do. These are useful expressions with grammar inside them.
  • Question focus: a table asks how long a person plays. The nearby time-of-day phrase does not answer duration. Read the interval, calculate the length, then express it in the permitted number of words.
  • Text-supported explanation: when asked why a person likes school, use the reason supplied by the passage; a generic positive judgement may be insufficient.
  • Editing: the photographed messages show spelling and pronoun inconsistencies. Use a small revision checklist rather than asking for more words immediately.

No audio was supplied, so listening performance cannot be evaluated from the answer sheet. Some handwritten answers and teacher marks are ambiguous; do not infer exact section scores or the reasons for every deduction. The visible total is not a proficiency diagnosis.

3. A gradual six-step bridge

  1. Identify referents and distinguish subject, object and possessive forms.
  2. Make the present-simple verb agree with the subject, including questions and negatives.
  3. Recall expressions as units: meaning, preposition and following verb form.
  4. Use grammar and logic together in short cloze contexts.
  5. Answer reading questions with evidence, duration/quantity calculations and word-limit control.
  6. Build and edit a short message, then review it with the teacher.

The app implements six corresponding practice steps. Each requires the selected 50 or 60 scored retrieval submissions and an 8/10 separate check before the next step becomes available. Attempts and correct responses are tracked separately. Open writing is saved locally for teacher review and is not automatically graded. The bank repeats and remains a starter resource, not a secure examination.

For classroom use, distribute repetitions across several short sessions. A count is a minimum practice rule, not proof of mastery. Mix familiar forms with new contexts and revisit a skill after a delay.

4. Chinese website research

An accessible 21世纪教育网 Grade 7 Zhejiang midterm simulation preview includes listening, reading, language application and writing, with word-form gaps and contextual tasks. It is a commercial sample preview, not a nationally mandated paper. Its coverage is specific to its stated textbook units. I reviewed the visible preview rather than accessing a paid download.

The official curriculum standards library supplies the national framework. Question order and local paper formats vary; one website and the supplied photographs cannot establish a universal Grade 7 sequence. An additional government-hosted search result returned 404 and was excluded from the evidence.

New app questions were authored for these skill patterns. The public app does not reproduce the photographed papers or publish a student's identifying information.

5. Vocabulary categories and the eventual IELTS bridge

At Grade 7, compare accessible words along a meaningful dimension: cheap (price), useful (function), convenient (ease) and valuable (worth). They belong in a comparison network but are not interchangeable synonyms.

Later, compare damage (harm), undermine (weakening a foundation or confidence), compromise (impairing standards, safety or integrity) and jeopardize (placing at risk). Explain typical collocations and different senses; “a compromise” can also describe a settlement. These are advanced extensions, not evidence that Grade 7 pupils should already use every word.

Reference entries: Cambridge: undermine and Cambridge: jeopardize. The app's definitions and examples are original paraphrases.

IELTS Academic assesses listening, reading, writing and speaking. The app's advanced bridge is preparation practice; its completion percentages are not IELTS band estimates.
